1.open: Who is someone from your past, like a teacher, neighbor or coach, who quietly made a difference for you, even if they never got credit?
questions: Verse 7 says the Israelites "were fruitful and increased rapidly." Why might a chapter that begins with a growing family end up in such a dark place?
Verse 8 says "a new king, who did not know Joseph, came to power." How quickly can kindness and good history be forgotten, in a nation, a workplace or a family?
The king says the Israelites are "too numerous and too powerful for us" (v. 9). What does fear tend to do to the way people treat those they see as a threat?
Verse 12 says "the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and flourished." Where have you seen good things grow in a hard season, even when it did not feel that way at the time?
Verses 13 and 14 describe lives made "bitter with hard labor." What do you think the people were feeling? If you have ever felt stuck or unseen by God, how would you put that honestly?
We are told the midwives "feared God" and so they "let the boys live" (v. 17). What do you think it means to fear God here, and how might that fear shape what a person does under pressure?
Shiphrah and Puah are named, while the powerful king is not (vv. 15, 17). Why might the writer remember the names of two ordinary women? Who are the quiet, unnamed people doing right in your world?

Christians read the midwives' answer to Pharaoh in different ways, some seeing a justified lie and others seeing courage with a flaw (v. 19). How do you think about it, and what do you do when obeying authority and doing what is right pull apart?
1.life: Think of one person who is overlooked or treated unfairly where you work, study or live. This week, do one small, concrete thing for them, like a kind word, a seat at your table or speaking up for them.
1.prayer: Thank God that he sees people who are crushed and does not forget them. Ask for the courage of Shiphrah and Puah to quietly do the right thing, and pray for anyone you know who feels trapped right now.
1.tip: Questions 5 and 8 can pull the group into a debate about lying or about civil disobedience. Say briefly that Christians disagree about the midwives' answer, then steer back to what the text clearly shows: God honored their reverence. Give quiet or doubting people room to say that God feeling absent in suffering is a real experience, and don't rush to fix it.

2.open: Who is someone who looked out for you when you were young, even in a small way?
questions: Moses' mother "saw that he was a beautiful child" and hid him for three months (v. 2). What do you notice about the risk she took, and what do you think drove her?
His sister "stood at a distance to see what would happen to him" (v. 4). Have you ever had to wait and watch while someone you love was in a situation out of your control? What was that like?
Pharaoh's own daughter "had compassion on him" (v. 6), and the river meant to kill him became his rescue. Where have you seen help come from a surprising person or place?
Moses grew up in the palace but "went out to his own people" and saw their hard labor (v. 11). Why might it matter that he went to look, and what are we tempted to look away from today?

Moses looked "this way and that" and then killed the Egyptian (v. 12). Christians differ on whether this was a justified defense of the oppressed or a rash act of violence, and the chapter leaves it open. What do you make of it?
A fellow Hebrew asked, "Who made you ruler and judge over us?" (v. 14). When has your effort to help been rejected or gone wrong? How did you handle it?

Moses named his son Gershom, saying, "I have become a foreigner in a foreign land" (v. 22). Have you ever felt out of place or far from where you thought your life would be? Say as much or as little as you like, including if God has felt distant.

Verse 24 says "God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant." What does it mean to you that God hears the cry of people who feel stuck, and what do you find hard about waiting for him to act?
2.life: This week, notice one person who is hurting or overlooked, in your family, workplace or neighborhood. Pray for them by name each day, and ask God whether there is one small, wise thing you can do to help.
2.prayer: Thank God that he hears, sees and takes notice of those who cry out. Ask him to help you trust him in seasons of waiting, and to show you who around you needs compassion.
2.tip: The killing in verse 12 may pull the group into a long debate. Say plainly that Christians read it differently and that the text neither praises nor condemns Moses. Then steer back to the bigger picture: God was working through ordinary people long before Moses was ready.

3.open: Have you ever been asked to take on a job or favor you felt totally unqualified for? What happened?
questions: Moses was out tending sheep when he noticed the bush and said, "I must go over and see this marvelous sight" (v. 3). What gets your attention these days, and how do you tend to respond when something unexpected interrupts an ordinary day?
God says, "Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground" (v. 5). What does this moment tell us about who God is and how Moses is meant to approach him?

God says, "I have indeed seen the affliction of My people in Egypt" and "I am aware of their sufferings" (v. 7). What does it mean to you that God sees and hears before he acts? Has there been a time you needed to know that?
Moses answers, "Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh?" (v. 11). What reasons do people give today for feeling unqualified to serve God or help others? Which ones sound most like you?
God does not list Moses' strengths. He says, "I will surely be with you" (v. 12). How is a promise of God's presence different from a boost of confidence?

In verse 14 God says, "I AM WHO I AM." Christians read this in different ways: some hear mainly that God is unchanging and self-existent, others hear mainly a promise that he will be present with his people. What stands out to you in this name, and what do you make of the mystery in it?

In verses 21 and 22 the Israelites leave Egypt carrying silver, gold and clothing, and the text calls it plundering. Many see it as fair pay for years of forced labor, and others find it uncomfortable. How do you read it, and how do you handle parts of the Bible that sit uneasily with you?
If you are honest, is it easier right now to trust that God sees you, or that he is with you? What would help, even a little?
3.life: Pick one thing you have been putting off because you feel unqualified. Take one small step on it this week, and each day say to God, "I will surely be with you" (v. 12) as a reminder of what he promised Moses.
3.prayer: Thank God that he sees and hears the suffering of his people. Ask him for a sense of his presence in whatever you feel unprepared for, and pray for anyone in the group who is carrying a heavy load.
3.tip: Verse 14 can pull the group into a long debate about Hebrew and philosophy. Name in one line that Christians read it differently, then bring people back to the story: God hears, God comes down, and God promises to be with Moses. Also give a moment of quiet for anyone who wonders why God saw the suffering for so long before acting, and do not rush to answer it.

4.open: What is something you were asked to do once that you felt completely unqualified for?
questions: Moses asks, "What if they do not believe me or listen to my voice?" (v. 1). What are you most afraid people will think when you try to speak up for what matters to you?
God asks, "What is that in your hand?" (v. 2). It was only a shepherd's staff. What ordinary thing in your own life might God be able to use?

Moses says, "I have never been eloquent" (v. 10). Some think he had a speech problem and others think he was simply out of practice after years away. Either way, what are the reasons you give when you feel unfit for something?
God answers, "Who gave man his mouth?" (v. 11), and then promises, "I will help you as you speak" (v. 12). How does that answer fit with the worry Moses actually had?

Moses finally says, "Please, Lord, send someone else" (v. 13), and "the anger of the LORD burned against Moses" (v. 14). Yet God still gives him Aaron. What does that tell you about how God deals with our fears?
Be honest here: is there something you sense God may be asking of you, or something you are unsure about, where you are making excuses or simply feel stuck? What makes it hard?

Verses 24 to 26 are some of the strangest in the Bible, and even scholars are unsure of the details. Many think it has to do with Moses not having circumcised his son. What do you do with a passage that leaves you with more questions than answers?

At the end the people "believed" and "bowed down and worshiped" when they heard that the LORD "had seen their affliction" (v. 31). Why might it matter so much to hear that God has seen what you are going through?
4.life: Think of one thing you have been putting off because you feel unqualified. This week, take one small step toward it, or ask one trusted person to help you with it, the way Moses was given Aaron.
4.prayer: Tell God honestly about the excuses you tend to make. Thank him that he sees the suffering of his people, and ask for the help and the people you need to say yes to what he asks.
4.tip: Verses 24 to 26 may pull the whole discussion off course. Say plainly that it is a puzzling scene and that scholars are unsure of the details, offer the common reading about circumcision in a sentence, and then bring the group back to Moses and his excuses. Also be gentle with anyone who relates to Moses too well; they may be quietly afraid, so let them speak without hurrying to fix it.

5.open: Tell about a time you tried to fix something and it got worse before it got better.
questions: Moses and Aaron say, "Let My people go, so that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness" (v. 1). What does it tell you that God's first request is about worship and not only about escape?
Pharaoh answers, "Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice?" (v. 2). When have you heard people ask a question like that, or asked it yourself, about God?

Pharaoh calls the people "lazy" and tells the taskmasters to "make the work harder" so they will "pay no attention to these lies" (vv. 8, 9). Why might a powerful person try to keep others too busy and worn out to think about worship or freedom?
The people had to scatter "to gather stubble for straw" while keeping the same quota (v. 12). Where do you see people today being asked to do more with less? Where do you feel that in your own life?
The foremen were beaten, then went to Pharaoh and got nowhere (vv. 14 to 18). Why do you think they turned on Moses and Aaron afterward, saying they had been made "a stench before Pharaoh" (v. 21)?

Moses asks God, "Why have You brought trouble upon this people? Is this why You sent me?" (v. 22). What do you notice about the fact that Moses says this straight to God, and that the text does not scold him for it?
Moses says, "You have not delivered Your people in any way" (v. 23). Have you ever felt that way about a prayer or a hope? If you would rather not say what it was, just say what it felt like.
When doing the right thing seems to make life harder first, what helps you keep going, or helps you work out whether to stop?
5.life: Think of one honest complaint or question you have been holding back from God. This week, say it to him plainly, the way Moses did, and then be quiet for a minute and listen.
5.prayer: Thank God that we can bring our hardest questions to him. Ask for patience and trust for anyone in the group who feels stuck in a hard season, and pray for those who are overworked or treated unfairly.
5.tip: The chapter ends with no answer, because God's reply starts in chapter 6. Some people will want to hurry to a happy ending. Resist that, let the discomfort sit, and treat Moses' blunt prayer as permission for quieter members to be honest too.

6.open: Think of a time when someone gave you good news but you were too tired or discouraged to take it in. What was that like?
questions: God tells Moses, "Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh" (v. 1). Why might God start with a promise about what he will do, instead of a command about what Moses must do?
God says, "I have heard the groaning of the Israelites" and "I have remembered My covenant" (v. 5). What does it mean to you that God hears and remembers? When have you needed to hear that?
In verses 6 to 8 God makes a string of promises: bring out, deliver, redeem, take, and give. Which one stands out to you, and why?
Verse 7 says, "I will take you as My own people, and I will be your God." What does it mean for God to belong to people like that, and for people to belong to him?

Moses told the Israelites God's message, but "on account of their broken spirit and cruel bondage, they did not listen" (v. 9). Why can hopeful words be hard to hear when life is crushing? What helps, and what only makes it worse?

Moses says, "I am unskilled in speech" (v. 12). What do you feel unqualified or unready for? If you're honest, what part of this story is hard for you to believe, or has God felt quiet in your own life?
God does not argue with Moses about his speech. He simply gives Moses and Aaron their charge (v. 13). What do you notice about how God deals with Moses' doubt?
The chapter pauses for a long family list (vv. 14 to 25). Why might the writer want us to know that Moses and Aaron were real people from a real family, with ordinary ancestors?
6.life: Think of one person who is worn down right now. This week, don't offer them a speech. Offer something practical, like a meal, a ride, a note or your time, and let your presence say that they have not been forgotten.
6.prayer: Thank God that he hears the groaning of his people and remembers his promises. Ask him to help anyone in the group who feels too tired or discouraged to hope, and to give us honest trust even when we feel unqualified.
6.tip: The name "the LORD" in verse 3 can send the group down a rabbit hole, since Genesis already uses it and scholars read it differently. Say in a sentence that interpreters differ, then steer back to the heart of the chapter: God hears, remembers and promises, even when people are too crushed to listen. Also don't rush past verses 14 to 25. Treat the list as a reminder that God works through real families, and move on.

7.open: Tell about a time you dug in and refused to back down, even when you suspected you were wrong.
questions: God says to Moses, "See, I have made you like God to Pharaoh" (v. 1). Moses had said he was a poor speaker. Where have you felt unqualified for something God seemed to be asking of you?
Moses was eighty and Aaron eighty-three when they spoke to Pharaoh (v. 7). What does it say about God that he sent them at that age, after so many years of waiting?
God says, "the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD" (v. 5). Why do you think God wants even Pharaoh and Egypt to know who he is?
The magicians "also did the same things by their magic arts" (v. 11), yet Aaron's staff "swallowed up the other staffs" (v. 12). What do you make of this contest, and why might the writer include it?
The Nile was Egypt's source of water, food and livelihood. What do people we know rely on for security the way Egypt relied on the Nile?
Pharaoh "did not take any of this to heart" (v. 23), while ordinary Egyptians dug for water (v. 24). Who ends up paying for one powerful person's stubbornness, and where do you see that today?
Christians read the hardening of Pharaoh's heart differently. Some see God deciding it, others see God confirming a stubbornness Pharaoh already chose. What questions does this raise for you?
If you are honest, when has the evidence in front of you been hard to accept? What made it hard to change your mind, and what helped, if anything?
7.life: This week, think of one thing you have been stubborn about, such as a conflict, a habit or a question you have avoided. Tell God about it honestly, and take one small step toward listening.
7.prayer: Ask God to give us soft hearts that can still listen. Pray for people who are suffering because of other people's choices, and for anyone in the group who feels unqualified for what lies ahead.
7.tip: The hardening of Pharaoh's heart will likely dominate the talk. Name in one line that Christians disagree, note that the text also says Pharaoh's heart was hardened as his own response, then steer back to the question of how we respond when we hear God. Also welcome honest doubts about the plagues without rushing to answer them.

8.open: What is the most annoying small pest you have ever had to deal with, like mosquitoes, ants, mice or something else?
questions: God's demand is the same each time: "Let My people go, so that they may worship Me" (v. 1). Why do you think the goal is worship and not only escape?
The magicians "did the same thing by their magic arts" (v. 7), yet all they did was bring more frogs. What are some things people turn to for help that end up adding to the problem?
Pharaoh says, "Pray to the LORD to take the frogs away from me" (v. 8). Why do you think he asks for prayer only when things get bad? When have you done something similar?
Moses tells Pharaoh the timing is up to him "so that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God" (v. 10). What do you think God wanted Pharaoh, and the Israelites watching, to learn?

Verse 15 says that "when Pharaoh saw that there was relief, however, he hardened his heart." Why is it so easy to forget a promise once the pressure is gone? Where have you seen that in your own life?
The magicians finally say, "This is the finger of God" (v. 19), and Pharaoh still will not listen. What do you think it takes for someone to move from seeing evidence to actually trusting?

God says, "I will make a distinction between My people and your people" (v. 23). What might it have meant for the Israelites to see that God knew exactly where they were? If you are honest, how does that feel when your own situation seems unnoticed?
Pharaoh keeps trying to bargain: worship here, or do not go very far (vv. 25, 28). What are some ways we offer God a smaller version of what he asks?
8.life: Think of one promise you made to God or someone else when things were hard and have let slide since. This week, take one small, honest step toward keeping it, or tell God plainly where you are with it.
8.prayer: Thank God that he hears us when we call, even when we are slow to trust him. Ask for a heart that stays soft when the pressure lifts, and pray for anyone in the group who feels unnoticed right now.
8.tip: Questions about Pharaoh's hardened heart may lead the group into a debate about free will and God's role. Say plainly that Christians understand it differently, since the text describes it both ways, then bring the group back to Pharaoh's pattern of promising and retreating, which everyone can recognize in themselves.

9.open: Think of a time you said sorry mainly because you were caught or things were going badly. How did it feel afterward?
questions: Three disasters come in this chapter: sick animals, boils and hail. Which one stands out to you, and why?

Twice God makes a clear difference between Israel and Egypt (vv. 4, 26). Pharaoh even sends officials to check, and still "he would not let the people go" (v. 7). Why do you think evidence alone did not change his mind?

God tells Pharaoh, "I have raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power to you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth" (v. 16). What do you think God wants Pharaoh and the world to learn about him?

God gives a warning before the hail, and some officials "feared the word of the LORD" and brought their servants and livestock inside, while others "disregarded" it (vv. 20, 21). What do you think made the difference between them?
Pharaoh admits he has sinned, calls the LORD righteous, and says that he and his people are wicked (v. 27). Those are strong words. Why might they still not amount to real change?
Moses answers, "I know that you still do not fear the LORD our God" (v. 30). What is the difference between being sorry about consequences and being sorry about what we did?

The chapter says both that Pharaoh "hardened his heart" (v. 34) and that "the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart" (v. 12). Christians read this differently. How do you make sense of the two, and where are you unsure?
Where in your own life have you put off doing something you knew was right, hoping the pressure would pass? What helps you move from knowing to doing?
9.life: This week, think of one thing you have been putting off, such as an apology, a decision or a change. Take one small real step toward it, and tell God honestly where you are with it.
9.prayer: Ask God for a heart that listens the first time and not only when things get hard. Pray for anyone in the group who feels stuck or stubborn in something right now.
9.tip: This chapter has hard scenes of suffering, and some people will struggle with how God treats Egypt. Don't rush to defend or explain. Let people say what troubles them, and point to what the text itself highlights: God's warnings, his patience, and his care for the Israelites. On the hardening of Pharaoh's heart, say plainly that Christians disagree and keep the focus on the whole chapter.

10.open: Have you ever put off something you knew you needed to do, like a phone call or a doctor's visit? What finally got you moving?
questions: God says the signs are so that "you may tell your children and grandchildren" what he has done (v. 2). What stories of God's help have been passed down to you, in your family or your church?
Moses asks Pharaoh, "How long will you refuse to humble yourself before Me?" (v. 3). What makes humbling ourselves so hard, even when we can see the damage of holding out?
Pharaoh's own officials say, "Egypt lies in ruins" (v. 7). Why might the people closest to a stubborn person see the cost sooner than the person does?
Pharaoh offers to let only the men go (v. 11), and later everyone but the animals (v. 24). What does it look like today to give God part of our lives while keeping something back?

Pharaoh says, "I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you," yet when the locusts are gone he refuses again (vv. 16, 20). What is the difference between being sorry about the consequences and being sorry about the wrong?

The chapter says both that God hardened Pharaoh's heart (v. 1) and that Pharaoh refused to humble himself (v. 3). Christians read this differently: some see God deciding Pharaoh's response, others see God confirming a stubbornness Pharaoh had already chosen. What questions does it raise for you?
In the darkness, "all the Israelites had light in their dwellings" (v. 23). Where have you sensed God's care in a dark or confusing time, or where are you still waiting to sense it?
Moses says, "we will not know how we are to worship the LORD until we arrive" (v. 26). What is one area where God is asking you to trust him before you can see the whole way?
10.life: Think of one thing you have been giving God only partly, such as time, money, a habit or a relationship. This week, take one honest step toward giving it fully, and tell someone in the group what it was.
10.prayer: Ask God to soften any place where we have grown stubborn, and to give us a humble heart that turns back to him for real. Thank him that he sees his people, even in the dark.
10.tip: The hardening of Pharaoh's heart will likely spark debate. Say in one line that Christians differ, point to both verses 1 and 3 in the text, and bring the group back to the question of what they are holding back themselves.

11.open: Think of a time you were warned about something and waited too long to act. What happened?
questions: God says one more plague will come, and then Pharaoh "will allow you to leave this place" (v. 1). After so many plagues and broken promises, what do you think it was like for the Israelites to hear that an end was near?

The text says the LORD "gave the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians" and that Moses was "highly regarded" (v. 3). Why might it matter that ordinary Egyptians and officials saw things differently from Pharaoh?

Moses announces that "every firstborn son in the land of Egypt will die," from Pharaoh's household to "the servant girl behind the hand mill" (v. 5). Why do you think the text names both the highest and the lowest? How do you react to such a hard passage?
Verse 6 says a "great cry will go out over all the land of Egypt." What do you think the writer wants us to feel here, and what do you feel as you read it?

In verse 7, "not even a dog will snarl at man or beast" among the Israelites, so that they "will know that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel." What would that stillness have meant to a frightened family on that night?

Verse 10 says the LORD "hardened Pharaoh's heart." Elsewhere in Exodus Pharaoh hardens his own heart, and Christians understand how the two fit together in different ways. What questions does this raise for you?
When a ruler's stubbornness brings suffering on ordinary people who had no say, who do you think is responsible? Where do you see that happen in the world today?
If you are honestly unsure what to make of God in this chapter, what is one question you would like to ask him, or one thing that troubles you?
11.life: Pay attention this week to people who suffer because of decisions they did not make. Choose one person or group to pray for by name each day, and, if you can, do one small practical thing to help.
11.prayer: Thank God that he sees the oppressed and keeps his promises. Ask him for honesty about the hard parts of Scripture, and for mercy for people who suffer because of the choices of others.
11.tip: The death of the firstborn is difficult, and some people may be upset or quiet. Do not rush to defend or explain it away. Let people say it is hard, point out that the text itself does not soften it, and keep the group looking at what the chapter says about God's justice and his care for Israel. Say plainly that Christians differ on verse 10.

12.open: What is a family meal or tradition from your childhood that you still remember, and what is the story behind it?
questions: God tells Moses, "This month is the beginning of months for you" (v. 2). Israel's calendar starts with being rescued. When have you felt like you were given a fresh start?
Each household was to choose a lamb and keep it for several days before the meal (vv. 3, 6). What might it have been like to live with that lamb in your home, knowing what was coming?
They were to eat "fully dressed for travel" (v. 11). Are you more ready to move when God calls, or more likely to want to stay in what is familiar? Why?

God says, "when I see the blood, I will pass over you" (v. 13). Christians read the blood in different ways: some see a substitute dying in the place of the firstborn, others see mainly a protective mark on the household. What does this detail show you about how God rescues?
Parents are told what to say when children ask, "What does this service mean to you?" (v. 26). Who first told you about God, and how would you explain what God has done for you to someone younger?

The text says "there was no house without someone dead" (v. 30). It does not soften this. What does this verse stir up in you, and how can we hold rescue and grief together? It is fine to say you are unsure or troubled.

Verse 49 says, "The same law shall apply to both the native and the foreigner who resides among you." A "mixed multitude" also left Egypt with Israel (v. 38). What does this tell you about who is welcome at God's table?
12.life: This week, tell one story of a time God helped you to someone else, maybe a child, a friend or a neighbor, the way verses 26 and 27 describe. If you like, share a simple meal with flatbread while you tell it.
12.prayer: Thank God for rescuing his people, and for the ways he has rescued you. Ask for honesty about the parts of this chapter that are hard, and for compassion toward people who grieve.
12.tip: Verses 29 and 30 are the hard spot. Don't rush to explain or defend them. Let people say it is troubling, and point out that the text itself records the weeping. Then gently return to what the chapter shows about God and Pharaoh's oppression, without forcing an answer in one evening.

13.open: What is a family tradition you grew up with, and do you know where it came from?
questions: Moses tells the people, "Remember this day, the day you came out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery" (v. 3). Why do you think God wants them to keep remembering, and not just be glad once?

Parents are told to explain the festival to their children: "This is because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt" (v. 8). Who told you the stories of your faith, and how did they do it?
Verse 14 pictures a child asking, "What does this mean?" What questions about faith did you ask as a child, or are you still asking now?
God claims every firstborn, but sons are redeemed, or bought back (v. 13). What does it tell us about God that he sets up a way to buy back rather than take?

The firstborn laws point back to the night when "the LORD killed every firstborn in the land of Egypt" (v. 15). Many readers find this hard to hold alongside a loving God. What do you honestly think and feel when you read it?

God did not lead them by the shorter road, because "they might change their minds and return to Egypt" (v. 17). Have you ever looked back on a long, hard route and seen a reason for it, or are you still waiting to see one?
Moses took the bones of Joseph with him (v. 19), keeping a promise made long before. What promises from the past, to people or from God, are you carrying today?
The LORD went before them "in a pillar of cloud to guide their way by day, and in a pillar of fire" by night (v. 21). When have you felt guided, and when have you felt like the guide was hard to see?
13.life: Pick one small way to pass on a memory of God's faithfulness this week. Tell a child, a friend or a neighbor about a time God helped you, or write it down to keep.
13.prayer: Thank God for leading his people out of slavery and for going ahead of them. Ask him to help you remember his faithfulness and to guide you on a road you do not understand.
13.tip: Verse 15 and the death of Egypt's firstborn may stir hard feelings. Let people say what they feel without rushing to explain it away, then point to the redemption of the firstborn sons as the chapter's focus. Also note that Christians read the firstborn laws and the sign on hand and forehead in different ways, and that is fine.

14.open: Think of a time you got stuck somewhere with no easy way out, like a traffic jam, a locked door or a dead battery. What happened?
questions: The LORD tells Israel to turn back and camp with the sea in front of them (vv. 1-2). Why might that have felt like a strange or even foolish instruction to the people?
When Pharaoh's army appears, the people are "terrified and cried out to the LORD" (v. 10). Then they turn on Moses. What does this show about how fear works in us?

They say, "It would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness" (v. 12). Why can a hard, familiar place start to look better than an uncertain freedom? Where have you felt that pull?
Moses says, "The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still" (v. 14). Then the LORD says, "Tell the Israelites to go forward" (v. 15). How do being still and going forward fit together?
The pillar of cloud moves behind the people and stands between the two camps (vv. 19-20). What does it tell you about how God cares for his people in the dark?

The chapter says the LORD "hardened" Pharaoh's heart (v. 8), and Christians understand that differently. Some say God overrode Pharaoh's will, and others say he confirmed a stubbornness Pharaoh had already chosen. What questions does this raise for you?
The sea closes and "not one of them survived" (v. 28). The text is blunt about it. How do you honestly respond to this part of the story, including any discomfort or doubt?
At the end the people "feared the LORD and believed in Him" (v. 31). What do you think helps trust grow: seeing God act, or something else?
14.life: Name one situation this week where you feel stuck or afraid. Each day, pray about it, and ask what the next small step forward might be. Take that step, even if the whole path is not clear yet.
14.prayer: Thank God that he goes before us and behind us. Ask for steady trust where you feel cornered, and pray for anyone in the group facing something that looks impossible.
14.tip: Verse 28 and the hardening of Pharaoh's heart may stir strong feelings. Don't rush to explain them away. Say plainly that Christians read these verses differently, let people voice discomfort honestly, and bring the group back to the chapter's main thread: God rescues people who cannot save themselves.

15.open: What is a time you were so relieved after something stressful that you felt like celebrating, and how long did the good feeling last?
questions: The song says, "The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation" (v. 2). When have you felt that God was your strength, or given you a reason to sing?
Moses and the people give God the credit for the rescue and say, "The LORD is a warrior" (v. 3). Why might it matter that they sing about what God did instead of what they did?

The Egyptians boasted, "I will pursue, I will overtake" (v. 9), and the song celebrates their defeat. How do you feel about a song of victory over an enemy, and how do you hold that alongside Jesus' call to love our enemies?
The song ends, "The LORD will reign forever and ever!" (v. 18). What difference does it make to say God reigns when life feels out of control?
Miriam is called "the prophetess" and leads the women in tambourines and dancing (v. 20). What helps you celebrate what God has done, and how could our group do more of it together?
Only three days after the song, "they walked in the desert without finding water" and then found bitter water (vv. 22, 23). Why do you think relief fades so quickly when the next problem shows up?
The people grumbled, "What are we to drink?" (v. 24), and Moses cried out to the LORD. When you are thirsty, disappointed or doubting, what do you do with your complaints? Be as honest as you like.

Christians read the sea crossing differently. Some take it just as described, and others see a poetic telling of a real escape. Whichever way you read it, what does the song want its singers to remember? And what do you make of God saying, "I am the LORD who heals you" (v. 26)?
15.life: Israel went from the sea to Marah to Elim in a few days. This week, when a problem shows up, take a minute to name one way God has helped you before, out loud or on paper, and then bring the new problem to him.
15.prayer: Thank God for rescues, big and small, that you have already seen. Ask him to be your strength and your song when the water tastes bitter, and pray for anyone in the group who is in a dry stretch.
15.tip: The song celebrates the Egyptian army drowning, and some people will find that uncomfortable. Don't rush to smooth it over. Let people say what bothers them, point out that the song is sung by people who were just rescued from slavery, and let the group sit with the tension without forcing a tidy answer.

16.open: What is one meal from your childhood that you still think about, and why?
questions: The people say, "There we sat by pots of meat and ate our fill of bread" (v. 3). They are remembering slavery as a good time. Why do we sometimes remember hard seasons as better than they were when the present feels uncertain?
Moses tells them, "Your grumblings are not against us but against the LORD" (v. 8). Where do you see complaining in your own life, and who usually hears it?
God answers the complaining with food, not with punishment. If that surprises you or is hard to believe, what makes it so? Be as honest as you like.
God says, "Each day the people are to go out and gather enough for that day" (v. 4). What would it be like to live on daily supply instead of a stockpile?
Verse 18 says "he who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall." Where are you most tempted to store up for safety, whether money, time, plans or control?
God says, "Understand that the LORD has given you the Sabbath" (v. 29). He calls it a gift. What does real rest look like for you, and what gets in the way?
Aaron is told to keep a jar of manna "for the generations to come" (v. 33). What would you keep to remind your family or friends of a time God came through for you?
16.life: Pick one stretch of time this week, even a few hours, to rest on purpose. Put your phone and to-do list away, and each time you feel the urge to catch up, thank God for one thing he has already given you today.
16.prayer: Thank God for daily bread, and for patience with our complaining. Ask for trust to receive today's portion without fear of tomorrow, and pray for anyone in the group who is anxious about provision right now.
16.tip: Someone may ask whether the manna was a natural desert food or a pure miracle. Christians differ on that, so say so in a line and move on to the heart of the chapter: God provides, and he teaches trust one day at a time. Also be gentle with the complaining. The people were hungry and afraid, so let the group see themselves in it instead of looking down on Israel.

17.open: When did you last feel really thirsty or tired, and what was the first thing you wanted?
questions: The people had followed God's direction and still found no water (v. 1). Why does it hit so hard when things go wrong right after we did what we thought God asked?
The people said, "Why have you brought us out of Egypt" just to die of thirst (v. 3). What do you think was really behind their anger, besides thirst?
Moses cried out, "What should I do with these people? A little more and they will stone me!" (v. 4). What do you notice about where Moses takes his frustration?
God does not punish the people. He tells Moses to strike the rock, and water comes out (vv. 5, 6). What does that tell you about how God responds to people who doubt?
The place is named for the question, "Is the LORD among us or not?" (v. 7). When have you quietly wondered something like that? What would count as an honest answer for you?
Israel wins only while Moses keeps his hands up, and Aaron and Hur hold them steady when he grows tired (vv. 11, 12). Who has held you up when you were worn out, and who might you hold up?
The LORD says he will "utterly blot out the memory of Amalek" (v. 14). Christians understand this harsh vow differently. How can we read it honestly without rushing past it?
Moses names the altar "The LORD Is My Banner" (v. 15). What do you rally around when life feels like a fight?
17.life: This week, when you catch yourself grumbling or doubting, say the question plainly to God, asking whether he is really with you in this. Then ask one person to stand beside you in something hard, or offer to do that for someone else.
17.prayer: Thank God for meeting thirsty, doubting people with water. Ask him to show you his presence where you feel alone, and pray for anyone in the group who is tired and needs help holding their hands up.
17.tip: Verses 14 to 16 can pull the whole evening into the question of God's vow against Amalek. Say in a sentence that Christians read it differently, then bring the group back to what the whole chapter shows: God providing, and people leaning on God and on each other.

18.open: Who is someone you trust to tell you the truth, even when it is not what you want to hear?
questions: Moses' sons were named for his story: "I have been a foreigner in a foreign land" and "The God of my father was my helper" (vv. 3, 4). If you named something after your own story, what would you call it?
Moses tells Jethro about "all the hardships they had encountered along the way" as well as the rescue (v. 8). Why might it matter to tell the hard parts of a story and not only the good parts?
Jethro says, "Now I know that the LORD is greater than all other gods" (v. 11). What have you seen or heard in someone else's story that made God seem more real to you?
Moses says the people come to him "to inquire of God" (v. 15). He is doing real, good work. Why do you think it is so easy for a good person to end up carrying far too much?

Jethro says, "What you are doing is not good" and "You cannot handle it alone" (vv. 17, 18). Where in your life, at home, work, church or school, do you feel stretched thin? What makes it hard to ask for help?
Jethro wants leaders who are "capable," "God-fearing, trustworthy," and "averse to dishonest gain" (v. 21). Why do you think character is listed alongside ability?

Jethro offers his plan humbly: "If you follow this advice and God so directs you" (v. 23). Moses, the great leader, "listened to his father-in-law" (v. 24). What helps you listen well when someone points out a blind spot?

Be honest here: when someone tells you that you are doing too much, or doing it the wrong way, what do you usually feel first? Is there a part of you that finds it hard to let go or trust others with the work?
18.life: Pick one task you have been carrying alone, at home, work or church. This week, ask one trustworthy person to share it with you, or ask someone you respect to tell you honestly where you are stretched too thin.
18.prayer: Thank God for the people who care enough to speak honestly to us. Ask for humility to hear good advice, and for wisdom to share the load with others.
18.tip: Questions 5 and 8 can stir up guilt in people who already feel overworked or who think asking for help is a weakness. Say plainly that Moses was not failing; he was faithful and needed help. Also note that Christians read Jethro's faith in verse 11 differently, as a first step toward faith or as confirmation of a faith he already held, and leave it there.

19.open: Have you ever been somewhere so grand or powerful, like a huge storm, a canyon or a packed stadium, that it made you feel small? What was it like?
questions: Before God asks anything of Israel, he says, "You have seen for yourselves what I did to Egypt, and how I carried you on eagles' wings and brought you to Myself" (v. 4). Why do you think God starts with what he has already done?
God says that if they obey, "you will be My treasured possession out of all the nations" (v. 5). What does it mean to you to be treasured, and is that easy or hard to believe about yourself?
God calls the people "a kingdom of priests and a holy nation" (v. 6). What do you think it means for a whole people to stand between God and the world around them?
The people answer together, "We will do everything that the LORD has spoken" (v. 8). Have you ever promised more than you could deliver? What does that make you think about this moment?

Christians read the condition in verse 5 differently. Some see a deal based on keeping the law, set against grace. Others see obedience as a thankful response to a rescue already given. Which way of reading helps you, and why?

The people wash their clothes and prepare for two days, and a boundary is set around the mountain (vv. 10-12). What do these steps say about who God is? How do we get ready to meet God today, if we do at all?
When God comes down, "all the people in the camp trembled" (v. 16). Is it possible for God to be both close and caring and yet overwhelming? Have you ever felt something like that?
Honestly, how do you feel about a God who sets boundaries and warns people to keep back (vv. 21-24)? Say it however it comes, whether it is awe, fear, confusion or doubt.
19.life: Set aside ten quiet minutes this week, with no phone, to simply be in God's presence. Start by remembering one specific way God has carried you through something, then notice how it feels to come close.
19.prayer: Thank God for carrying his people and bringing them to himself. Ask for both a deep reverence for who he is and the confidence to come near.
19.tip: Verses 12 and 13 (death for touching the mountain) and verse 15 can feel harsh or strange. Don't rush to defend or explain them away. Say that they stress how holy God is and how serious it is to approach him, admit that they are hard to read, and move on to the bigger picture of God's rescue and invitation.

20.open: What is a rule from your childhood home that you still follow today, even though no one is making you?
questions: Before any command, God says he is the one "who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery" (v. 2). How does it change the way you hear the commands to know the rescue came first?
"You shall have no other gods before Me" (v. 3). Most of us don't bow to statues. What do people today lean on for security, identity or happiness that can slowly take God's place?

God calls himself "a jealous God" (v. 5) and also promises "showing loving devotion to a thousand generations" (v. 6). What does the word jealous bring to mind for you, and does the picture of a faithful marriage help?

"Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy" (v. 8). The day of rest covered the whole household, servants and animals too. What would real rest look like in your week, and what gets in the way? Christians differ on how the Sabbath applies today, so there is room for different answers here.
Verses 12 to 16 protect family, life, marriage, property and honest speech. Which of these do you think our culture takes most seriously, and which does it take lightly?
The last command goes inside a person: "You shall not covet" (v. 17). Why might God care about what we want, and not only what we do?

The people trembled and said, "Speak to us yourself and we will listen" (v. 19). When you think about God honestly, do you feel closer to afraid, curious, distant or something else? Any honest answer, including doubt, is welcome.
20.life: Choose one rhythm of rest this week, even just a few unhurried hours with the phone put away. Use that time to thank God for what he has already done for you, the way chapter 20 opens.
20.prayer: Thank God that he rescues before he asks anything of us. Ask him to show you anything that has quietly taken his place, and to give you rest and honest trust.
20.tip: The line about punishing children to the third and fourth generation (v. 5) and the people's terror can unsettle some in the group. Point to the same verses where God's love reaches a thousand generations and where Moses says "Do not be afraid" (v. 20), and let people say plainly what troubles them without rushing to fix it.

21.open: Think of a rule you grew up with, at home or at school, that seemed unfair at the time. Looking back, what do you think of it now?
questions: The chapter opens with laws about servants (v. 1). Verse 2 says a Hebrew servant "shall go free without paying anything" in the seventh year. What stands out to you about how this law treats a person who is poor and in debt?

In verses 7 to 11, a daughter sold as a servant is protected: her master "must allow her to be redeemed" if she displeases him, and if he withholds food, clothing or marital rights, "she is free to go without monetary payment" (vv. 8, 11). What do these protections tell us about how God sees the vulnerable, and what do they leave unsettled?

Verses 18 to 19 say a person who injures someone in a fight must pay for lost work and see that the other is "completely healed." Where do you see that idea of making things right, rather than only punishing, in your own life or community?

Verse 21 says a master is not punished if a servant survives a day or two, "since the servant is his property." Verses 26 and 27 free a servant who loses an eye or a tooth. How do you react to a law that protects people and still uses this language?

Many Christians read these laws as God limiting harsh practices people already had, while others read them as accepting those practices for that time. Which reading do you find more natural, and what questions does it leave you with?

"Eye for eye, tooth for tooth" appears in verses 24 and 25. Many read it as telling judges to match the penalty to the harm and go no further. How is that different from how we often respond when we are hurt?

Verses 28 to 36 say an owner who was warned about a dangerous ox and did nothing is responsible (v. 29), and so is someone who leaves a pit uncovered (v. 33). Where do carelessness and ignoring a warning cause harm today, and who ends up paying?
Some of this chapter is hard to read, and honest people feel uneasy about parts of it. What in this chapter troubles you or confuses you, and what do you do with that unease?
21.life: This week, look for one place where someone has less power than you, such as a coworker, a child, a neighbor or someone you serve. Ask what you could do to make sure they are treated fairly, and do one small thing about it.
21.prayer: Thank God that he cares about people with the least power and protects them. Ask him to make you attentive to anyone being overlooked, and honest about the parts of Scripture you find hard.
21.tip: Verses 20 to 21 and the slavery laws will bring strong reactions, and someone may want to defend or dismiss them quickly. Read the verses aloud, say plainly that Christians disagree on what the laws show, and let people name their discomfort without rushing to resolve it. Verse 22 is also read in different ways, so if it comes up, note that translations differ and move on.

22.open: Have you ever lent something to a neighbor or friend and gotten it back damaged, or not at all? What happened?
questions: Verse 3 says "A thief must make full restitution." Why might paying back what was taken, and more, do something that only punishing the thief would not?
In verse 6, the person who started a fire must pay for the grain it burned, even if he never meant any harm. What does this say about taking responsibility for the effects of our actions?
In verses 10 and 11, when there are no witnesses, the matter is settled by "an oath before the LORD." What does that tell you about how much honesty and trust mattered in Israel's daily life?

Some laws in this chapter, like verses 16 and 17, speak mostly about the woman's family and say little about her own voice. How do you handle parts of the Bible that feel strange or uncomfortable to us today? Be as honest as you like.

Verse 18 says "You must not allow a sorceress to live," and it was later used to justify killing people accused of witchcraft. Why is it important to ask how a verse has been used, and what it meant to its first hearers, before we apply it?

Verse 21 says "You must not exploit or oppress a foreign resident, for you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt." Why does God ground this command in Israel's own memory? Where does remembering your own hard times help you treat others well?
Verses 22 to 24 say God hears the cry of widows and orphans and takes it personally. Who do you think is in a similar position today, and what, if anything, do you think a society owes them?

Verses 26 and 27 say a borrowed cloak must be returned by sunset because it was the only covering the man had, and God adds, "I am compassionate." What does it tell you about God that he cares about a blanket? Is that easy or hard for you to believe about him?
22.life: Pick one practical way this week to look out for someone with little protection or power, such as a newcomer, a widow, a single parent or a struggling neighbor. Offer a meal, a ride, a listening ear or a fair deal. If you owe anyone something, whether money, an apology or a returned item, make it right.
22.prayer: Thank God that he hears the cry of people who have no one else, and that he is compassionate. Ask him to show you who around you needs someone on their side.
22.tip: The strange laws in this chapter, especially verses 16 to 20, can pull the whole evening off track. Name them honestly, say that Christians read them with care and sometimes differ, and then steer the group back to the heart of the chapter in verses 21 to 27. Also note that interpreters differ on whether verses 8 and 9 send disputes to human judges or to God at the place of worship, because the Hebrew word can mean either. You do not need to settle it.

23.open: Think of a time someone returned something you lost, or went out of their way to help you. What happened?
questions: Verse 1 says, "You shall not spread a false report." Where do rumors and half-truths spread most easily today: at work, in families, online? What makes them so tempting to pass along?
Verse 2 says, "You shall not follow the crowd in wrongdoing." Describe a time it was hard to disagree with the people around you. What helps someone stand alone?
Verses 3 and 6 warn against favoring the poor in court and also against denying them justice. Why might God ask for fairness in both directions, and what does that say about what justice is?
Verses 4 and 5 tell Israel to help the animal of someone who "hates you." What would the modern version of that look like, and what would make it hard for you?
Verse 9 says, "you yourselves know how it feels to be foreigners." When have you been the outsider? How did it shape the way you treat newcomers or people on the edge?

Verses 10 to 12 build rest into the farm year and the work week, for the poor, for animals and for workers. What does this say about how God sees rest? What is one honest obstacle to resting well in your own life?

In verses 20 to 33 God promises to guide Israel and drive out the peoples of Canaan. Christians read this hard section differently, so how can we be honest about what troubles us in it while still listening to what the chapter says about God's care and Israel's loyalty?
If you are unsure how much of this ancient law connects to your life, or whether God is as just and caring as this chapter says, what questions or doubts would you like to put on the table?
23.life: Pick one concrete act from the first half of the chapter. Correct a rumor you have heard, help someone you find difficult, or take a real rest. Do it this week and note how it felt.
23.prayer: Ask God to make you fair, honest and kind to the outsider, including people you find hard to like. Thank him for rest, and ask for help trusting him with the parts of this chapter that are hard to understand.
23.tip: Verses 23 to 33 may pull the whole discussion into the question of God ordering nations driven out. Say plainly that Christians understand it differently, give it one question's worth of time, then bring the group back to the justice, rest and care for outsiders that fill most of the chapter.

24.open: Think of a promise you made out loud to someone, like a wedding vow, a team pledge or a handshake deal. What made it feel serious?
questions: God tells Moses to bring Aaron, Nadab, Abihu and seventy elders, but they are to "worship at a distance" (v. 1). Moses alone comes near. What does this layering of nearness tell us about how Israel understood God?

The people all answered together, "All the words that the LORD has spoken, we will do" (v. 3). Why do you think it felt easy to say yes? When have you promised something with great sincerity and found it harder to keep?
Moses "wrote down all the words of the LORD" (v. 4) and later read the Book of the Covenant aloud (v. 7). Why might it matter that the terms were written and heard, not just felt?
Moses says, "This is the blood of the covenant" (v. 8). Blood is a striking thing to use in a ceremony. What do you think it was meant to show the people about how serious this promise was?

Christians hear an echo of this verse in Jesus' words at his last meal about the blood of the covenant. How does that connection change the way you read this scene, or does it raise questions for you?

The leaders "saw the God of Israel," yet "God did not lay His hand on the nobles of Israel; they saw Him, and they ate and drank" (vv. 10-11). What strikes you about a holy God welcoming people to a meal?

The glory of the LORD looked "like a consuming fire" to the people below (v. 17), and Moses disappeared into the cloud for forty days (v. 18). If you were waiting at the bottom, what would be going through your mind? Be honest about any mix of awe, fear, doubt or boredom.
The people made their promise out loud, together, in front of one another. What difference, if any, does making a commitment in front of others make to whether it holds?
24.life: Pick one commitment you have made, to God or to someone else, and take one small step this week to keep it. If it feels too heavy to carry alone, tell one person in the group and ask them to check in with you.
24.prayer: Thank God for drawing near to people who could not come close on their own. Ask for honesty about the promises we struggle to keep, and for trust in his mercy when we fall short.
24.tip: The group may stumble over the blood ritual in verses 6 to 8 because it feels strange or even disturbing today. Do not rush past it or over-explain it. Say that blood stood for life and for a promise too serious to break, let people voice their discomfort, and keep returning to what the text itself says: God makes a covenant with his people and invites them to his table.

25.open: Think of a place that feels special to you, like a house, a room, a spot outdoors. What makes it feel that way?
questions: God asks for an offering from "every man whose heart compels him" (v. 2). Why might God want gifts that are freely given instead of required? How does that shape the way you think about giving?
The list in verses 3 to 7 includes gold, yarn, wood, oil and spices. What do you notice about it, and what might it say that God asks people to give ordinary materials, not only precious ones?
Verse 8 says, "so that I may dwell among them." What does it tell us about God that his stated goal is to live with his people?

Three times God stresses the pattern he showed Moses, ending with "according to the pattern shown you on the mountain" (v. 40). Why do you think the details mattered so much, and what do they say about approaching God?
The poles were to "remain in the rings of the ark" (v. 15) so it could always be carried. What does a God who travels with his people say to you about seasons of change or moving on?

God says, "I will meet with you there above the mercy seat" (v. 22). What do you make of a God who sets up a place to meet people and speak with them? When have you felt close to God, or far from him?

The bread was to sit "before Me at all times" (v. 30), and the lampstand gave light in the holy room. If you feel unsure what you believe about God being near, what would you honestly want to ask him?
This chapter is full of gold and careful craftsmanship. Where do you see the same care and beauty in the way people serve or worship today, and where do you see it missing?
25.life: God wanted to live among his people. This week, set aside one small, regular time and place, even ten minutes at a kitchen table, to be quiet and talk with God. Notice what it is like to make room for him.
25.prayer: Thank God that he wants to be with his people. Ask him to make you generous and willing, and to help you notice his presence in ordinary places this week.
25.tip: The furniture details can feel dry, and the group may drift into debate about whether each item points to Christ. Christians differ on that. Say so briefly, then steer back to the big idea in verse 8: God wants to be close to his people. Question 7 is the gentle one for anyone who is unsure.

26.open: Think of a place you have lived or stayed that felt like home. What made it feel that way?
questions: This chapter is mostly measurements, materials and instructions. What is your honest reaction to reading it, and what do you think it is doing in the Bible?
The inner curtains were made of "finely spun linen" with "cherubim skillfully worked into them" (v. 1). Why might God want a place of such care and beauty, even in a desert?

The outside was goat hair, ram skins and leather (vv. 7, 14), plain and tough, while the inside was rich. What do you make of that contrast, and where have you seen something plain on the outside hold something precious?
The tent was built to be taken apart and carried, yet it had to be sturdy. What does it say about God that his dwelling place traveled with his people?
Verse 30 says to set it up "according to the pattern shown you on the mountain." Why might it matter that Moses was not free to design it his own way?
The veil "will separate the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place" (v. 33). What does that barrier say about who God is, and how does it make you feel about approaching him?
Christians have read the veil in light of the temple curtain torn when Jesus died, as a sign that the way to God is open. How does that change the way you read this chapter?
If you are unsure what to make of a God who lives in a tent, or wonder if he is near at all, what would you honestly say about where you sense God's presence, or its absence?
26.life: Set aside ten quiet minutes this week in one spot, with phone away, simply to be with God. Notice what makes that place feel set apart, and what gets in the way.
26.prayer: Thank God that he chose to live among his people and not far off. Ask him to make you aware of his nearness this week, including in ordinary places.
26.tip: The detail can make people's eyes glaze over, so do not read every measurement aloud. Summarize each section in a sentence and spend your time on the questions. On the symbolism, Christians differ on how much each detail points to Jesus, so say so in one line and keep moving.

27.open: Think of a place you go to when you need to be quiet or feel close to something bigger than yourself. What makes it feel that way?
questions: God tells Moses the altar must be built "just as you were shown on the mountain" (v. 8). Why do you think God cared about getting the pattern right? What does that say about how he wants to be approached?

The altar was made of wood covered in bronze, with a horn on each corner (v. 2), and it was where sacrifices were burned. Why might a place of sacrifice be the first thing a person met on the way to God?
The altar had poles and rings so it could be carried (v. 7). What does that tell you about the kind of God Israel was following, and the kind of life they were living?

The courtyard was fenced with linen curtains, yet ordinary Israelites could come in with their offerings, while only priests went further into the tent. What do you notice about who was welcomed and who was kept back?
The plain white walls had one entrance, with a curtain of "blue, purple, and scarlet yarn" (v. 16). Why might God give a single, beautiful way in instead of many?

Some Christians read the altar and gate as pictures pointing to Jesus and his death. Others see them mainly as the practical setting for Israel's worship at that time. How do you tend to read details like these, and what do you gain from each approach?

The people were to bring oil "to keep the lamps burning continually" (v. 20), and the priests tended them "from evening until morning" (v. 21). What do you make of a light that someone stays up to look after through the night?
Be honest: when you read chapters full of measurements and materials, what do you feel? Is there anything here that helps, confuses, or leaves you cold?
27.life: This week, set aside one small, regular time and place to be quiet before God, even five minutes. Treat it like tending a lamp: show up, keep it simple, and notice what it is like to make room on purpose.
27.prayer: Thank God that he made a way for ordinary people to come near him. Ask him to make you steady in the small, unseen habits of faith, and to help anyone in the group who feels far away.
27.tip: The measurements and materials can make eyes glaze over. Don't read every detail aloud or try to decode every symbol. Focus on a few big ideas: God sets the pattern, a way in is provided, and someone keeps the light on. If the symbolism question comes up, say plainly that Christians read it differently and move on.

28.open: Is there a uniform, outfit or piece of clothing that makes you feel different when you put it on, whether it is a work shirt, a wedding dress, or a favorite jacket?
questions: God says the garments are "to give him glory and splendor" (v. 2). Why might God want the people to see their priest dressed this way? What does it say about how God sees worship?
Aaron is to "bear their names on his two shoulders as a memorial before the LORD" (v. 12). What do you notice about carrying names, not just serving as a representative?

Verse 29 says Aaron will carry the names "over his heart" whenever he enters the Holy Place. What does it tell you about God that the names were kept close to the heart and not just written on a list?
The Urim and Thummim (v. 30) are mentioned briefly, and no one today knows exactly what they were or how they worked. How do you handle parts of the Bible that leave questions unanswered?

The robe had bells that would be heard when Aaron entered or left, "so that he will not die" (v. 35). That sounds severe to many readers. What does it show about how people in that time understood coming near God, and how do you react to it?
The gold plate read "HOLY TO THE LORD" and Aaron wore it "so that they may be acceptable before the LORD" (vv. 36, 38). Why do you think the people needed someone else to carry that for them?

Many Christians read the priest carrying the people's names as a picture of Jesus standing before God for us, while others see the chapter mainly as a record of how Israel's worship was arranged. Whichever way you lean, what does this chapter stir in you about being represented before God?
If you are not sure you believe God is near or cares, what in this chapter do you find hard to accept, and what, if anything, draws you in?
28.life: Each day this week, take a few minutes to name before God, one by one, people you care about, as if carrying their names on your shoulders. Pray for one person a day, and tell them if it seems right.
28.prayer: Thank God that he knows his people by name and keeps them close to his heart. Ask him to help each person in the group bring someone else's need before him this week.
28.tip: The detail about gems, chains and rings can feel dry, and verse 35 can sound harsh. Don't rush through or defend every point. Spend your time on the names carried on the shoulders and over the heart (vv. 12, 29), and say plainly that Christians differ on how much of the chapter is symbol.

29.open: Think of a time you were officially welcomed into something, like a new job, a team, a church or a family. What do you remember about that day?
questions: God starts with washing, special clothes and oil, all done at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting (vv. 4-7). Why might it matter that this was done in public and not in private?
Aaron and his sons were to "lay their hands" on the head of the bull and each ram (v. 10). What do you think that action said about them and the animal?
The bull is a sin offering for the priests themselves, and it is burned "outside the camp" (v. 14). What does it tell you that the people who serve God needed this first?

Blood was put on the right ear, thumb and big toe of each priest (v. 20). Many readers see this as giving the whole person to God: what they hear, what they do and where they go. Which of those three do you find hardest to hand over?

The priests ate part of the ram and bread at the doorway (v. 32), and the rest was burned if it was left over (v. 34). What do you notice about a meal that is shared in the place where God meets people?

The ceremony and the daily lambs were repeated, one lamb in the morning and the other at twilight (vv. 38-39). What does it say about God and about us that this was meant to be regular and not a one-time event?

God says, "I will dwell among the Israelites and be their God" (v. 45). This is the reason for everything else in the chapter. What does it mean to you that God wants to live among people? If you are unsure about that, what makes it hard to believe?
Christians differ on how much of this chapter points ahead to Jesus. Whichever way you lean, what do you take from a priesthood that began with such care and cost?
29.life: Pick a morning or evening time this week and set aside five minutes, as Israel did at dawn and dusk, to be quiet before God. Say what is on your mind, honestly, in your own words.
29.prayer: Thank God for wanting to be close to his people. Ask for a heart that notices him in the ordinary rhythms of the day, and pray for those in your group who lead or serve others.
29.tip: The animal sacrifices and blood can feel strange or off-putting, and some may stall there. Do not rush past that reaction. Name it as an honest one, then steer the group back to the point God gives at the end of the chapter: he wants to meet with his people and live among them (vv. 45-46). If the Jesus connection comes up, say plainly that Christians read it differently and leave it there.

30.open: What is a smell that instantly takes you back to a particular place or person?
questions: The incense altar is placed where God says, "where I will meet with you" (v. 6). What does it say about God that he sets a place and a way to meet his people?
Incense was to burn "perpetually before the LORD" (v. 8), morning and evening. What daily or weekly habits help you stay close to God, and which ones feel like a struggle?

Verse 15 says "the rich shall not give more than a half shekel, nor shall the poor give less." What do you make of a rule where everyone pays the same? What might it have meant to a poor family, and to a wealthy one?
The census payment is called a ransom "for his life" (v. 12). Why might God want every person to be counted and covered in the same way?
The priests had to wash "so that they will not die" (v. 20). That sounds severe to us. How do you react to it, and what does it suggest about how seriously the text treats coming close to God?

Verses 29 to 33 show the oil setting things and people apart as holy, and no one could copy it for ordinary use. What do you think it means to be set apart for God, and where do you see that idea in your own life?
Verses 37 and 38 forbid making the incense "to enjoy its fragrance." What is the difference between enjoying God and treating holy things as something for our own pleasure?
If you are honest, does this chapter make God feel close or far away to you right now? What in the text, or in your own life, makes you say that?
30.life: Pick a regular time each day this week, such as morning coffee or the drive home, and use it as your own small moment to meet with God. Even a few quiet minutes counts. Notice what you bring to him.
30.prayer: Thank God that he makes a way for people to come near to him. Ask for a steady habit of turning toward him each day, and for honesty about where you feel distant.
30.tip: Verses 20 and 33 can sound harsh, and someone may say God seems unfair here. Let them say it. Don't rush to defend or explain it away. Note that the text stresses how serious God's holiness is, and that Christians also differ on how far to read these objects as pictures of Jesus. Bring the group back to what the chapter shows: God provides a way to meet him.

31.open: What is something you made or fixed with your own hands that you were proud of?
questions: God says he has called Bezalel by name and "filled him with the Spirit of God" (v. 3). What stands out to you about God using a craftsman, rather than a priest or a prophet, for this job?
Verse 6 says, "I have also given skill to all the craftsmen." What does it say about God that he cares about skill in metal, wood and stone?
Bezalel leads and Oholiab assists, and many other workers are named only as a group. Where have you seen people serve well in a role that few people notice?
What is one ability you have, whether it is cooking, listening, fixing things, organizing or something else, that you rarely think of as a gift from God? How might it serve others?
God calls the Sabbath "a sign between Me and you for the generations to come" and "the LORD who sanctifies you" (v. 13). What do you think it means for rest to be a sign of who God is?

Right after the long list of building work, God says the Sabbath must still be kept, a "Sabbath of complete rest, holy to the LORD" (v. 15). Why might God put this reminder here, and where does work or busyness crowd out rest in your life?

Verse 17 says that on the seventh day God "rested and was refreshed." What does real rest look like for you, and what makes it hard to take? If you feel unsure that rest is for you, or that God cares about it, you can say so honestly.
31.life: Choose a block of time this week, even a few hours, and set work aside on purpose. Use it for something that restores you, and thank God for it.
31.prayer: Thank God for the gifts and skills he gives his people, and ask him to show you how to use yours. Ask for the trust to rest, and for help letting go of the need to keep going.
31.tip: The penalties in verses 14 and 15 will trouble some people, and scholars are unsure what "cut off" meant. Christians also differ on how the Sabbath applies today. Say so briefly, then bring the group back to the heart of the passage: God provides gifted workers, and God gives rest as a sign of his care.

32.open: Think of a time you waited much longer than expected for something, like a late ride, a slow answer or a delayed flight. What did you do to fill the time?
questions: The people said, "we do not know what has happened to him!" (v. 1). When God or a leader or a hope feels silent for a long time, what do people tend to reach for to fill the gap?

Aaron announced, "Tomorrow shall be a feast to the LORD" (v. 5). Many scholars think the calf was meant to represent Israel's own God, not a different one. How can something be sincere and religious and still go wrong?
God says, "How quickly they have turned aside" (v. 8). Where have you seen a good start drift off course faster than anyone expected, in a person or in yourself?

Moses argues with God and appeals to the promises made to Abraham, Isaac and Israel (vv. 11-13). What does it tell you that God lets Moses speak this way? What would it look like for you to be this honest in prayer?

Verse 14 says "the LORD relented from the calamity He had threatened." Christians read this differently: some think prayer truly changed God's course, others think God's purpose was fixed and the threat drew out Moses' plea. What do you make of it, and what do you find comforting or confusing about either view?
When Moses was confronted, Aaron said, "out came this calf!" (v. 24), though verse 4 says he shaped it himself. Why is it so easy to excuse ourselves this way? What helps us tell the truth instead?

Verses 27 and 28 describe the Levites killing about three thousand people. It is a hard scene, and the story does not soften it. What questions or feelings does it stir in you, and which of them would you be willing to bring honestly to God?

Moses says, "please blot me out of the book that You have written" (v. 32). He is willing to share the cost for people who failed. Christians have often seen this as pointing ahead to Jesus. What do you notice about a leader who stands with people instead of walking away?
32.life: This week, notice one moment when waiting or silence tempts you to grab a quick substitute, such as a screen, a purchase, a distraction or a worry. Instead of just fighting the urge, tell God plainly what you are feeling, the way Moses did.
32.prayer: Thank God for being patient with people who wander. Ask for honesty about what we reach for when we are waiting, and pray for someone you know who feels far from God right now.
32.tip: Verses 27 to 29 will likely stop the conversation, and some people will be troubled or angry. Do not rush to explain it away or defend it. Say plainly that it is a hard passage, let people name their reactions, and point back to what the chapter keeps showing: God takes sin seriously, and Moses pleads for the people anyway.

33.open: Where do you feel most at home, and who is usually with you there?
questions: God says he will still give the land but, "I will not go with you" (v. 3). The people heard "this bad news" and mourned (v. 4). Why would it feel like bad news when the promised land was still on offer?
The people took off their jewelry as a sign of grief (v. 6). What does it look like today to show that we are truly sorry, and not just embarrassed?

Moses set up a tent outside the camp, and "anyone inquiring of the LORD would go to the Tent of Meeting" (v. 7). Why might it matter that the tent was open to anyone and that you had to walk out to it? What does it take for you to step out and seek God?

Verse 11 says the LORD spoke to Moses "face to face, as a man speaks to his friend." What makes a friendship close, and what would that look like with God? If God feels distant to you right now, you are welcome to say so honestly.
Moses says that unless God's Presence goes with them, "do not lead us up from here" (v. 15). Where are you tempted to want what God gives more than God himself?
God answers, "My Presence will go with you, and I will give you rest" (v. 14). What would rest look like in your life right now, and what keeps you from it?
God says, "I will have mercy on whom I have mercy" (v. 19). Mercy is his to give freely. Does that comfort you, puzzle you, or both? Why?

God tells Moses he will see only his back, not his face (v. 23), and he covers Moses with his hand until he has passed by (v. 22). Why might a partial view be an act of care? Where have you seen only part of God's goodness so far?
33.life: Set aside ten minutes this week in a quiet place, your own tent outside the camp. Skip the requests list and simply tell God what is on your mind, as you would to a friend.
33.prayer: Thank God that he chooses to go with his people. Ask him to make you want his presence more than anything else he gives, and pray for anyone in the group who feels far from him.
33.tip: Many readers ask whether God really changed his mind because Moses pleaded. Christians differ on whether God changed his plan or whether the story describes an unchanging God in human terms. Say that in one line, then bring the group back to what is clear: Moses wanted God's presence most of all, and God gave it.

34.open: Think of something you broke, a dish, a phone, a plan. Did you try to fix it, replace it, or just live without it?
questions: God tells Moses to "Chisel out two stone tablets like the originals" (v. 1). The people broke the covenant, yet God begins again. What does it say about God that he starts again with the same people?

God describes himself as "compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness" (v. 6). Which of those words is easiest for you to believe about God, and which is hardest?
Verse 7 says God is "forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin," and also that "He will by no means leave the guilty unpunished." Why might it matter that both are true together?

Christians read the line about children and grandchildren in verse 7 in different ways. Some see God directly punishing descendants, others see how wrongdoing carries on in families. How have you seen the effects of one generation's choices reach the next?
