Moses "immediately bowed down to the ground and worshiped" (v. 8), then asks God to forgive "our iniquity and sin" even though the people are stubborn (v. 9). Why do you think he says "our" and not "their"?
Verse 21 says "on the seventh day you shall rest," even at plowing and harvest time. What makes rest hard for you, and what might it say about trusting God?

Moses "was unaware that his face had become radiant" (v. 29), and the people "were afraid to approach him" (v. 30). If you are unsure about God or find it hard to feel close to him, what would honest first steps toward him look like for you?
34.life: Think of one relationship where trust has been damaged, yours or someone else's. This week take one small, honest step toward repairing it, without pretending the hurt never happened.
34.prayer: Thank God that he is "compassionate and gracious" and keeps starting again with people who fail. Ask him to go with your group and to help each person take one honest step toward him.
34.tip: Verse 7 can derail the evening, since people may hear it as God punishing innocent children. Say up front that Christians read it differently, spend most of your time on the first half of the verse and on verse 6, and invite anyone with questions to keep talking afterwards.

35.open: What is something you once gave away or shared that you were glad about afterward?
questions: Before any building begins, Moses repeats the day of rest, "a Sabbath of complete rest to the LORD" (v. 2). Why might God put rest ahead of the work, even work on his own tent?

Verses 2 and 3 are hard to read, with a severe penalty for working on the Sabbath. Christians and Jews understand the fire rule in different ways. What questions or reactions come up for you as you read it?
Moses asks for gifts from "everyone whose heart is willing" (v. 5). What makes a gift feel freely given rather than expected or pressured, and does that difference matter to you?
The people came because their hearts "stirred" and their spirits "prompted" them (v. 21). Can you think of a time you felt that pull to give or help? What did you do with it?
Verse 22 says they gave "all kinds of gold jewelry." Jewelry was often a family's savings. What is the hardest kind of thing for you to give: money, time, energy or something else?

Notice who is named: "Every skilled woman spun with her hands" (v. 25), and Bezalel is given the Spirit of God along with skill for craftsmanship (v. 31). What does it say about God that he cares about skills like spinning, carving and weaving?

Bezalel and Oholiab were also given "the ability to teach others" (v. 34). What skill or ability do you have that could help someone else, even if it feels small or ordinary? And if nothing comes to mind right now, what makes it hard to see?
35.life: Look for one ordinary skill or possession you have and offer it to someone this week, such as a meal, a repair, a ride or an hour of your time. Give it freely, without keeping score.
35.prayer: Thank God that he welcomes gifts that come from a willing heart. Ask him to show you what you have to offer, and to loosen any grip that keeps you from giving freely.
35.tip: Verses 2 and 3 may stop the conversation because of the penalty. Don't rush past it or defend it. Say plainly that it is a hard verse, that Jewish and Christian readers understand the Sabbath and the fire rule differently, and then bring the group back to the main point of the chapter: willing hearts and gifted hands.

36.open: Think of a time you helped build or make something with other people, like a meal, a project or a repair. What did you enjoy most about it?
questions: Moses called the workers whose "heart stirred him to come and do the work" (v. 2). What do you think it looks like when someone's heart is stirred to serve, and when have you seen that?
Verse 3 says the people brought "freewill offerings morning after morning." Why might people keep giving day after day without being pushed?

The workers told Moses, "The people are bringing more than enough" (v. 5). Can you think of a time when a church, a family or a community had more than enough? How did that feel compared with how we usually talk about giving?
The people had to be "restrained from bringing more" (v. 6). Why might it be hard to stop giving or serving even when we are told there is enough? What would it take for you to step back gracefully?

The craftsmen made the curtains of "finely spun linen" with "cherubim skillfully worked into them" (v. 8). Why do you think God cared about beauty and skilled work in a place of worship? Where do you see skill used for God today?
Much of this chapter is measurements, clasps and wooden frames. If you are honest, how do you feel when you read a chapter like this, and what, if anything, does it show you about God?

The tent was built so it could be taken apart and carried (vv. 20-34), because the people were on the move. What does it say about God that he chose to be present with a traveling people rather than in one fixed place?

Christians read the tent in different ways. Some see its materials as pointers to Christ and the church, and others see mainly a worship space for Israel at that time. How might each view help you read a chapter like this with respect for the other?
36.life: This week, give something freely that nobody asked you for. It might be time, a skill or money. Notice how it feels to give from the heart rather than from duty.
36.prayer: Thank God for the gifts, skills and people he has put around your group. Ask him for a generous heart, and for the humility to know when to give and when to make room for others.
36.tip: Verses 8 to 38 are long lists of measurements and materials, and the group may glaze over. Read the key passages aloud, then turn quickly to the questions about giving and skill. If someone finds the details dull, say that is normal and invite them to share what stood out anyway. Keep the symbolism question light, since Christians read it differently.

37.open: What is something you own or made that you take extra care of, even though few people ever see it?
questions: Bezalel built the ark out of acacia wood and "overlaid it with pure gold, both inside and out" (vv. 1-2). Why might it matter that the gold was on the inside too, where almost no one would look?
The ark had rings and poles "in order to carry it" (v. 5). What does that tell you about how God wanted to travel with his people, and how they were to treat what was holy?
The two cherubim were "all made from one piece of gold" and faced "toward the mercy seat" (vv. 8, 9). What do you picture when you imagine this, and what do you think it said about meeting with God?
The mercy seat was where God met his people and where wrongs were covered once a year. Christians read this as pointing to Jesus. What does the word "mercy" mean to you personally?
The lampstand was "pure hammered gold, all of one piece" and shaped like almond blossoms (vv. 17, 19). Why do you think the craftsmen made something so detailed for a room only priests entered?
Much of this chapter repeats earlier instructions almost word for word. What can repetition like this show us about obedience, and how do you feel reading a long list of details?

Christians differ on whether each piece of furniture is meant to symbolize something about Jesus, or whether the point is simply that the people built exactly what they were told. Which parts of this chapter speak to you most, and which feel distant or hard to connect with?
Think of the ordinary work you do this week. Where might care and skill, even when unseen, be a way of honoring God?
37.life: Choose one task this week that no one will notice or thank you for, and do it with real care as an offering to God. Tell the group next time how it went.
37.prayer: Thank God that he wanted to live among his people and made a way to meet with them. Ask for a heart that cares about faithful, careful work, even when it is unseen.
37.tip: A chapter of measurements and furniture can feel dull, and some will say they don't see the point. Welcome that honestly, then steer toward verses 1 to 9 and the question of why care and meeting with God mattered. If symbolism comes up, say plainly that Christians differ and move on.

38.open: What is something you have helped build, fix or organize together with other people?
questions: The altar was built with poles "for carrying it" (v. 7). What might it say about God that his place of worship was made to travel with his people?

The basin was made from "the mirrors of the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting" (v. 8). Scholars are not sure what their role was. What do you notice about ordinary, personal things being given to God?
The only way into the courtyard was through a curtain "embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn" (v. 18). Why might God have wanted one entrance, and one that was beautiful?
The altar stands first in the courtyard, before anything else a worshiper would see. What does that tell us about how people approached God, and what do you make of it?

Christians differ on how much of this structure is a symbol pointing to Jesus. Some see meaning in nearly every detail, others read it mainly as a record of Israel's worship. How do you tend to read it, and why?

The silver came from "a beka per person, that is, half a shekel" (v. 26), the same for everyone. The gold was "from the wave offering" (v. 24), given freely. What does each kind of giving say about belonging to a community?
Verse 21 says, "This is the inventory for the tabernacle." The gifts were counted and recorded openly. Why might that matter, and how does your church or group handle money and trust?
Long lists of materials can feel dull or far away. What in this chapter is hard to connect with, and is there any small detail that caught your attention anyway?
38.life: Look for one quiet, behind the scenes job this week that nobody will praise, and do it as something given to God. It could be a task at home, church or work.
38.prayer: Thank God that he receives what ordinary people bring, from skilled work to simple gifts. Ask him to show you one thing you can offer freely this week.
38.tip: The numbers and measurements can lose people quickly. Don't read every figure aloud. Name the main picture (an altar, a basin, a fenced courtyard with one entrance, and open accounts) and move to the questions. If someone asks about the huge numbers, say honestly that scholars debate them and keep going.

39.open: Think of something you or someone you know made by hand, like a meal, a quilt, a repair or a garden. What made it special?
questions: Over and over the chapter says the work was done "just as the LORD had commanded Moses" (v. 5). Why do you think the writer keeps repeating this? What does it tell you about how these people saw their work?
The craftsmen hammered gold into thin sheets and cut it into thread to weave into the cloth (v. 3). What does that kind of patient, detailed effort say about how they viewed the task?

The onyx stones were engraved with the names of the sons of Israel and set on the priest's shoulders as "memorial stones" (v. 7). Why might it matter that the priest carried the people with him as he served?
The breastpiece held twelve stones, each engraved with one tribe's name (v. 14). Who do you picture being carried close to God's heart in prayer, and who might feel left out of that picture?

The gold plate on the turban read "HOLY TO THE LORD" (v. 30). What does it mean to you for a person or a place to be set apart for God? Does that idea feel encouraging, distant, or something else right now?
Verse 43 says Moses "inspected all the work" and then "blessed them." How does it feel to have your work noticed and blessed? When has someone done that for you, or when have you wished they would?
Christians read these details differently. Some see almost every piece pointing ahead to Jesus, and others see mainly a community's careful obedience. What do you notice in the chapter either way?
Most of this chapter is a list of fabric, metal and measurements. If you are honest, how do you respond to passages like this, and what, if anything, helps you stay with them?
39.life: Choose one ordinary task this week, like a chore, a work project or something you make for someone, and do it carefully and with attention as a quiet offering to God. Afterward, notice how it felt.
39.prayer: Thank God that he cares about the work of our hands and about each person by name. Ask for patience to do small things well, and pray for someone you want to carry close in prayer this week.
39.tip: A chapter of fabric and gemstone lists can make a group's eyes glaze over. Don't read every verse in detail. Highlight the repeated phrase about obedience, the names on the stones and the closing blessing, and let people admit if the details feel dull. Be ready for the question of what each stone is: say that no one is sure which modern gems the ancient names mean.

40.open: Think of a time you moved into a new home or space. What was the first thing you did to make it feel like yours?
questions: Moses is told to set up the tabernacle "on the first day of the first month" (v. 2). Why might it matter that this was a fresh start, after all that had gone wrong at Sinai?

Verse 16 says, "Moses did everything just as the LORD had commanded him." The chapter repeats this again and again. What do you notice about the way Moses works, and what does it say about how he saw his task?

Moses did not just build the tent. He used each item right away: he "arranged the bread," "set up the lamps" and "burned fragrant incense" (vv. 23, 25, 27). What is the difference between preparing for God and actually meeting with God, and where do you tend to stay on the preparing side?

Aaron and his sons were washed, dressed and anointed so they could "serve Me as a priest" (vv. 12 to 15). The basin was also there so they could wash "whenever they entered the Tent of Meeting" (v. 32). What do these details say about how people approached God then?

Verse 34 says, "the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle." This follows the golden calf, when it was unclear whether God would stay with Israel. What do you make of God choosing to dwell among a people who had failed so badly?

Verse 35 says Moses "was unable to enter the Tent of Meeting." Does the idea of being close to a holy God feel more like comfort or more like danger to you right now? Be as honest as you like, including if you aren't sure.
Israel only moved when the cloud lifted, and when it stayed, they stayed (vv. 36 and 37). Where in your life are you waiting for a sign, and where are you tempted to move ahead without one?
The book ends with the cloud and fire "in the sight of all the house of Israel through all their journeys" (v. 38). When have you sensed God's presence in a hard stretch, or wished you could?
40.life: Pick one regular, ordinary moment this week, like your commute, a meal or the first minutes after waking, and treat it as a small meeting place with God. Spend a couple of minutes there, even if all you say is that you are here.
40.prayer: Thank God for choosing to live among his people, even when they fail. Ask for a clear sense of his presence, and for patience to wait for his direction.
40.tip: Some will find the detailed lists dry, and Christians differ on how much symbolism to read into each item. Don't debate every object. Keep the group on the big picture: God is faithful to a people who failed him, and he comes to stay. Give quiet or doubting members room to say that God feels distant, since the chapter itself includes Moses being unable to enter.
